title: Short Stuff: Fahrenheit or Celsius
summary: Short Stuff episode on Fahrenheit versus Celsius. The hosts explain why -40 is the only temperature that is the same in both scales, using a graph/lapping analogy, and note that Celsius degrees are about 1.8 times larger than Fahrenheit degrees. They give the conversion formulas (multiply Celsius by 1.8 and add 32; subtract 32 and divide by 1.8 to go back) with a 20 C = 68 F example. They cover the history: Fahrenheit's invention in the early 1700s, Anders Celsius's proposal based on multiples of ten, the UK Met Office switching to Celsius in 1961, and the US sticking with Fahrenheit. They also mention that the National Weather Service uses Celsius internally but broadcasts in Fahrenheit. The episode opens with a callback to Simo Häyhä, the Finnish "White Death" sniper, from a listener-mail discussion.
topics: freezing and boiling points of water

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts joke about temperature units and introduce the topic of Celsius and Fahrenheit.

segments.title: Why conversion is selective
segments.summary: Hosts say they sometimes convert temperatures to Celsius on the show, and that the US uses Fahrenheit while most of the world uses Celsius.

segments.title: Simo Häyhä and the -40 listener mail
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh recall the Simo Häyhä episode mention, where listeners pointed out that -40 is the same in Fahrenheit and Celsius, and say they will explain why.

segments.title: Why the scales meet at -40
segments.summary: The hosts explain that Celsius degrees are larger than Fahrenheit degrees, so the two scales line up at -40, using a lapping-runners analogy and a graph explanation.

segments.title: Freezing and boiling points
segments.summary: Water freezes at 32 F and boils at 212 F, versus 0 C and 100 C in Celsius, which the hosts say makes Celsius easier to remember.

segments.title: Conversion formulas and examples
segments.summary: Explanation of converting Celsius to Fahrenheit by multiplying by 1.8 and adding 32, and the reverse; 20 C equals 68 F, and -40 is the same in both.

segments.title: Transition to history
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the question of why America still uses a system most of the world has dropped.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Break in the episode with a short sponsor segment.

segments.title: Countries using Fahrenheit and origins of the scales
segments.summary: Chuck notes the US, the Bahamas, Belize, and Palau still use Fahrenheit. Fahrenheit invented in the early 1700s by Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit, and Anders Celsius proposed a scale based on multiples of ten.

segments.title: UK switch to Celsius in 1961
segments.summary: Europe moved toward Celsius; the English-speaking world held on to Fahrenheit until the UK Met Office switched to Celsius in 1961, followed by former British Empire countries. The US kept Fahrenheit.

segments.title: National Weather Service units
segments.summary: The National Weather Service uses Celsius internally but broadcasts temperatures in Fahrenheit for American audiences; the hosts joke about public reaction.

segments.title: Wrap-up
segments.summary: Chuck says the episode was short and the hosts sign off.

segments.title: Credits and network tag
segments.summary: Closing credits noting the show is a production of iHeartRadio.
